title: Reconsidering Travel After Becoming a Parent
paragraphs: Having built much of his personal identity around frequent, adventurous international travel throughout his twenties, Faruq assumed parenthood would simply require modest logistical adjustments rather than a fundamental reconsideration of what travel itself could reasonably mean.

His first attempted trip with an infant, structured according to his previous independent travel habits, proved considerably more exhausting than rewarding, revealing that his prior approach was simply incompatible with a young child's needs and limitations.

Rather than abandoning travel entirely, as some exhausted parents around him had chosen to do, Faruq gradually developed an entirely different travel philosophy centered around slower paces, shorter distances, and deliberately reduced expectations regarding sightseeing volume.

This shift initially felt like a genuine loss, as the adventurous exploration he had valued so highly gave way to considerably more modest, child-paced experiences that bore little resemblance to his previous travel style.

Several years into parenthood, however, Faruq recognizes unexpected value in this slower approach, noting that lingering in fewer places allowed a depth of experience his previous rapid, ambitious itineraries had rarely permitted.

Reflecting on this evolution, Faruq suggests that travel's core value was never solely about covering maximum distance or destinations, a realization that required fundamentally rethinking assumptions he had never previously questioned during his earlier, more independent years.
